fatal_errors: The hypothesis replaces the AlCoCrFeNi plasma-sprayed coating and 550 °C post-anneal with unspecified thermal processing of duplex stainless steels.
It omits the target sulfuric-acid and cyclic molten-salt conditions and instead extrapolates broadly to irradiated high-temperature nuclear water without supporting evidence.
The cited evidence does not demonstrate thermally induced chromium surface enrichment or improved passivation; E2 instead describes phase-dependent microgalvanic selective dissolution.

The proposed thermal treatments could simultaneously alter phase balance, precipitates, grain structure, residual stress, and sensitization, so they do not isolate microsegregation as the governing variable.
explanation: The response addresses corrosion resistance in application-relevant steels and proposes measurable mediator and outcome variables, but it does not reconstruct the target material, coating process, annealing optimum, exposure conditions, or reported comparisons. Its only mechanistic overlap is the general role of chromium-rich passive films. The experiment has a useful same-composition control and employs XPS, SKP, electrochemistry, and mass loss, but lacks quantified processing and exposure windows and does not control major heat-treatment confounders. The falsification rule is also too weak because mediator formation without improved corrosion resistance should independently refute the claimed causal mechanism. Most importantly, the cited findings concern molten-chloride dealloying and microgalvanic phase contrast, not evidence that deliberately enhanced surface microsegregation creates a protective chromium-rich film.
